title: The Same Lie, Told a Second Time — Relapse, a Dream, Intercession
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. In the last lesson we saw a pair of hands that took hold of a man and would not let go, and we saw an old man standing on a mountain in the early morning, looking out at the smoke of a whole country going up.
And in the chapter we open today, the man who stood on that mountain and interceded for a city is himself the one who comes to grief.

So let me begin with an honest question. Is there an old fault in you that you have walked with for many years, and it is still there? Not something that flares up every day — but the moment pressure comes, out it walks with it.

Let me put the answer up front. A spiritual summit is no guarantee that you will not fall tomorrow. An old fault does not disappear by itself just because you have piled up experiences — and God's plan has never been held together by anybody's perfection.
1. The Same Lie, Twenty-Five Years Apart
Verse 1: "Abraham traveled from there toward the land of the South, and lived between Kadesh and Shur. He lived as a foreigner in Gerar."

"Traveled" is וַיִּסַּע (*vayisa*), which literally means to pull up the tent pegs and move on. And what he was moving away from was Mamre — the place where he had pleaded for a city, the place where he rose early in the morning and saw the smoke.
Then verse 2: "Abraham said about Sarah his wife, 'She is my sister.' Abimelech king of Gerar sent, and took Sarah."

Brothers and sisters, "she is my sister" — you have heard that sentence before. Genesis 12:13, down in Egypt: "Please say that you are my sister, that it may be well with me for your sake." The identical arrangement, word for word.
And the verb behind "took", וַיִּקַּח (*vayiqach*), is the very same word used in 12:15, where "the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house."
The same lie. The same consequence. Twenty-five years apart.

Brothers and sisters, I want you to think about what happened inside those twenty-five years. In chapter 15 God cut a covenant with him, and a burning torch passed down that path of blood. In chapter 17 God changed his name, the whole household was circumcised, and he himself took the knife at ninety-nine years old. In chapter 18 he stood and waited on three guests, and then pleaded for Sodom right down to the last count. In chapter 19 he saw the smoke of that judgement with his own eyes.
A covenant, a new name, a mark cut into his flesh, intercession, and the sight of judgement. All five of them, already behind him.
And then he arrives in Gerar, and out comes that sentence again.

This is a very important warning to us: spiritual experience does not automatically remove an old fault. You can have enormous faith in one area of your life and show not one inch of progress in another area for twenty-five years. And that old reflex usually does not appear on the peaceful days. It hides. It waits for the day the pressure comes, and then it walks out.
He tells the same lie twenty-five years later. Does that mean he had made no progress at all?

This chapter forces us to face something very uncomfortable: spiritual experience does not automatically repair a person's old fault. Standing in between those two occasions are a covenant, a change of name, circumcision, the pleading over Sodom, Yahweh himself appearing to him — nobody could call his experience shallow. And yet the moment pressure came, the thing he reached out and took hold of was the same old device. That is intensely practical for us: a person's real change is not measured at the peak experience, but in his first reaction when he is backed into a corner. So what needs dealing with is not one more conference. It is finding that old reflex, naming it, and giving somebody permission to ask you about it. And one more thing, in passing: this also warns us not to take a person's past experiences as a guarantee of his present judgement.
Abraham said Sarah was his sister, and half of that was actually true. Does it still count as a lie?

He explains himself in verse 12: "Besides, she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother; and she became my wife." So it was a half-truth. But Scripture's verdict on it could not be plainer — Abimelech says, "You have done deeds to me that ought not to be done!", and God says to Abimelech, "Now therefore, restore the man's wife." A half-truth is dangerous precisely because it can defend itself: the one who speaks it has a case ready in his own mind, while the one who hears it is led astray. That is very practical for us. When you are testing whether a sentence is honest, do not only ask, "Is anything in this sentence false?" Ask, "When I say this, do I want the other person to know, or do I want him not to know?"
2. A Light from the Original: A Foreign King's "Integrity of Heart and Innocence of Hands"
Verse 3: "But God came to Abimelech in a dream of the night, and said to him, 'Behold, you are a dead man, because of the woman whom you have taken; for she is a man's wife.'"

Brothers and sisters, notice the way God steps in. He does not go to Abraham first. He goes to the foreign king — and he goes in a dream. This is God's ordinary way of speaking to those outside the covenant: in chapter 31 he speaks to Laban like this, in chapter 41 to Pharaoh like this. A dream, every time.
Verse 4, and Abimelech's answer deserves to be read one sentence at a time: "Lord, will you kill even a righteous nation?"

"A righteous nation" is גּוֹי גַּם־צַדִּיק (*goy gam-tzaddiq*) — and that word "righteous", צַדִּיק (*tzaddiq*), is exactly the word Abraham used one chapter earlier when he was pleading: "Will you consume the righteous with the wicked?"

Brothers and sisters, the author has done this on purpose. In the previous chapter Abraham pleads for an unrighteous city; in this chapter a foreign king pleads his own innocence — and the two of them reach for the very same word.

Then in verse 5 he goes on: "I have done this in the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands." In Hebrew that is בְּתָם־לְבָבִי וּבְנִקְיֹן כַּפַּי (*betom-levavi uvniqyon kapai*). And when Psalm 24:4 asks who may stand on Yahweh's holy hill, the answer is "he who has clean hands and a pure heart" — the very same pair of words.

And here is the part that stings. The word behind "integrity", תֹּם (*tom*), comes from the same root as תָּמִים (*tamim*), the word God used in 17:1 when he told Abraham, "Walk before me and be blameless."
Brothers and sisters, do you see it? God told Abraham to be a *tamim* man — and in this chapter the one who says of himself that he is *tom* is a foreign king.
Then in verse 6 God says something enormously important: "Yes, I know that in the integrity of your heart you have done this, and I also withheld you from sinning against me."

God grants him his uprightness, and in the same breath says, "I also withheld you." Brothers and sisters, that single verse is saying two things at once: this man really was upright — and half of that uprightness is God's own hand holding him back.
And verse 7 is stranger still: "Now therefore, restore the man's wife. For he is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you will live."
The one who told the lie is the one called a prophet. The one who was deceived is the one told to go and ask him to pray.
Abimelech, a foreign king, says he acted in integrity of heart and innocence of hands, and God agrees with him. How are we to understand that?

In verse 6 God says, "Yes, I know that in the integrity of your heart you have done this, and I also withheld you from sinning against me." There are two things here worth holding on to. First, God works outside his own covenant people — a foreign king with no covenant at all behaved, in this matter, more uprightly than Abraham did. Second, God actively held him back, which means that his "not sinning" had God's keeping inside it too. So the warning cuts both ways. Do not imagine that believers are automatically the morally superior ones; and do not conclude from that that faith makes no difference at all — the difference lies in who has the God who will step in and stop a man. And the most awkward thing in this whole chapter is exactly this: Abraham gets rebuked by an outsider.
"Because I thought, 'Surely the fear of God is not in this place'" — why is that sentence the key to the chapter?

Because it is the real reason he lied: he assumed in advance that the other party had to be bad. He says so himself in verse 11. And the facts turn out to be the exact reverse — Abimelech fears God, and when he tells his servants what has happened, "the men were very scared" as well. So the problem was never the environment. The problem was his assumption. That is very useful to us, because the scripts we write in advance for other people are very often the starting point of our self-protective behaviour — and most of those scripts have never once been tested. Here is the practical step: the moment you notice yourself putting up a guard against someone, ask one question first — "Do I have any evidence for thinking this about him?" A great many defensive lies are told to fend off an attack that was never going to come.
3. Because I Thought the Fear of God Was Not in This Place

In verse 9 Abimelech summons Abraham and speaks to him with no politeness left in his voice at all: "What have you done to us? How have I sinned against you, that you have brought on me and on my kingdom a great sin? You have done deeds to me that ought not to be done!"
Brothers and sisters, a pagan king rebukes God's own chosen prophet in front of everyone. And the Bible writes it down without dropping a single word.
In verse 10 he asks a second time: "What did you see, that you have done this thing?"
And then comes verse 11, Abraham's reason — the one sentence in this whole chapter we ought to stand still in front of:
"Because I thought, 'Surely the fear of God is not in this place. They will kill me for my wife's sake.'"

Brothers and sisters, he made a spiritual assessment of the place: there is no fear of God among these people. And then, on the basis of his own assessment, he decided to arrange for his own survival himself.

And the result? This chapter proves that his assessment was wrong from top to bottom. This place had a king who answered God in a dream, who could say, "I have done this in the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands", who would name a prophet's fault in public, who then gave him sheep and cattle and male and female servants — and who said one very tender thing to Sarah.

Brothers and sisters, this is one of the commonest mistakes we make: we do God's assessment of the environment for him, and then we act on our own estimate. "That colleague is never going to listen." "That elder in my family will never believe, not in a hundred years." "That company simply has that kind of culture." We draw the boundaries on God's behalf, and then we work out our options inside the lines we drew ourselves.
And in verse 12 he adds one more thing: "Besides, she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother; and she became my wife."

So as a matter of fact the sentence was true. But brothers and sisters, a sentence in which every single word can be verified, spoken in order to make the hearer think something false — the Bible spends a whole chapter of consequences telling you what that is. The hardest lie of all to detect is the one in which everything said is true.
Abraham was the one in the wrong. Why does God still call him a prophet, and tell Abimelech to ask him to intercede?

Verse 7: "Now therefore, restore the man's wife. For he is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you will live." This is the first time the word "prophet" appears anywhere in the Bible — and it lands on a man who has just told a lie. What that verse is saying is this: the office is God's gift, not a man's earnings, and God did not withdraw what he had entrusted just because the man failed. Of course that is not to say a failure costs nothing. Verse 18 tells us that Yahweh had closed up tight all the wombs of Abimelech's household, and the whole affair had blown up across the entire town. So the two things have to be said together: God's grace does not revoke his calling, and a person's failure still has a bill to pay.
4. The Man Who Got It Wrong Is Still Called a Prophet
In verses 14 to 16 Abimelech gives Abraham sheep and cattle and male and female servants, restores Sarah his wife to him, and hands over a thousand pieces of silver on top of it.
Then verse 17: "Abraham prayed to God. So God healed Abimelech, his wife, and his female servants, and they bore children."
Brothers and sisters, look hard at how unbelievable that ending is.
The man in the wrong is Abraham. The household dragged into the damage is Abimelech's. And the way it gets resolved is this: the man in the wrong prays, and God heals.
God says it with his own mouth in verse 7: "For he is a prophet, and he will pray for you, and you will live."
This is grace — and it is a kind of grace that is very hard to swallow. God did not replace him because he had failed, and God did not suspend his office either.
And verse 18 says, "For Yahweh had closed up tight all the wombs of the house of Abimelech, because of Sarah, Abraham's wife."

Brothers and sisters, notice when all of this happens. The very next thing after this chapter is chapter 21 — Sarah conceives and bears Isaac. Which is to say: this whole affair takes place on the eve of the birth of the child of promise. Had Sarah remained in another man's house at that moment, that child's parentage could never have been settled, not for the rest of time.
So when God stepped in that night, it was not only to protect one woman's honour. It was to keep the line of the promise open.
And the way he protected that line was not through Abraham. It was around him.
I have done something wrong. Can I still go on serving?

Start by separating two categories. The first is weakness and failure — like the lie in this chapter. That needs confession, it needs putting right, it needs somebody to walk a stretch of road alongside you; but the office does not usually have to end because of it. The second is grave wrongdoing that disqualifies a person — anything criminal, anything that harms another person, anything that destroys trust. There you must stop, submit to the church's process, and put the protection of the person who was hurt first; "God is still using him" must never be used to skip over that. The questions that tell the two apart are these: has anyone been hurt by this? Has power been misused? And one more thing — restoration is never something a person announces about himself. It happens under the covering and the accountability of the community.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is softening Abraham's failure into "a small expedient". Some preachers reach this point and say, well, he was only trying to stay alive, that is only human. Brothers and sisters, he handed the mother of the child of promise over to another man's household — and he did it on the eve of her conceiving. That is not a small thing. If you soften it, your congregation will learn to find spiritual language for their own expedients.

The second is preaching God's restraint of Abimelech as God taking his own people's side. Look at the text: God calls Abimelech a man of "integrity of your heart", personally protects him from falling into sin, and then heals his whole household. What God protected was his promise — and in protecting it he also protected an innocent king. Preach it as favouritism, and your congregation's confidence in God's justice takes a cut.

The third is reasoning from "he is a prophet" to the conclusion that a leader may not be corrected. This entire chapter is a foreign king correcting a prophet in public, and Scripture writes it down without shaving off a word. Using your position to fend off a rebuke is turning grace into a talisman. Preach it that way and the problems inside a church become even harder to name.

The fourth is presenting "she is indeed my sister" as an acceptable technique. Scripture gives a half-truth no gentler treatment than an outright lie. And notice this: he did it twice, and his son Isaac does exactly the same thing in chapter 26. A weakness that never gets dealt with is handed on to the next generation.

The fifth is preaching the failure and never reaching the prayer. If this chapter stops at verse 13, all you have delivered is a scolding. Its real summit is verse 17 — the man who got it wrong, who was rebuked by an outsider, who has lost every shred of face, stands up and prays for somebody else, and God answers him. Your congregation needs to see that ending; without it, the next time they fail themselves they will not dare to serve again.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question. Chinese people are very afraid of losing face, so when something goes wrong the first thought is usually, how do I smooth this over? What does this chapter say to that? Brothers and sisters, the answer it gives is blunt: it cannot be smoothed over. Abraham's explanation comes in three layers — I thought there was no fear of God in this place; she really is my sister; and this was an arrangement my wife and I agreed on long ago. All three reasons hold up. Not one of them changes the facts. And the way the text handles it is fascinating: it lets the foreign king finish everything he has to say, and then it goes straight on to the prayer of verse 17. In other words, Scripture neither covers for him nor keeps beating him. That gives us a very good pattern: when something goes wrong, own it, and then go back to the thing you are supposed to be doing. Chinese culture tends to swing between two extremes — either never admitting fault at all, or admitting it and then collapsing entirely as a person. This chapter offers a third road.

The second question. An elder or a leader in my church has clearly done something wrong. Am I allowed to say so? Or would that be "disobedience"? Brothers and sisters, this chapter gives a very clear answer: a foreign king names a prophet's fault in public, and heaven does not rebuke him for it at all — on the contrary, God was the one who spoke to him first, in a dream. Galatians 2:11 says it even more directly: because Peter was in the wrong, Paul "resisted him to his face". So naming a problem is not the same thing as disobedience. But let me add three pastoral sentences. First, look at the motive. What Abimelech says is, "you have brought on me and on my kingdom a great sin" — his concern is the consequence, not revenge. Second, look at the setting and the procedure. Matthew 18 gives us the order: privately first. Third, look at what happens afterwards. Abimelech named the fault, and then went right on asking Abraham to pray for him — he did not destroy the man's office in the process. To be able to name a fault and not destroy the person: that is what maturity looks like.
At work, and among relatives, I often tell half the truth because I am afraid of losing out. How do I change that?

Three very practical steps. First, deal with the assumption underneath. Write down what you are assuming about that person, and then ask yourself what evidence you have for it. Abraham's lie grew straight out of an assumption with nothing under it. Second, have the honest sentence ready in advance. Most people tell a half-truth because in that moment they cannot think of a way to be honest without being rude — so think of it beforehand. Something like "I'm not free to talk about that just now" is far better than inventing a reason. Third, find a companion, tell him the situations in which you are most likely to be vague, and ask him to ask you about them. Honesty can be practised, and the way to practise it is to prepare the sentences, not to make the resolution.
7. Living 321 Out — No Longer Letting My Assumptions Decide Whether to Be Honest
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — God says, "he will pray for you, and you will live." A man who has just made a spectacular fool of himself is set between other people and God. And in Luke 23:34 the Lord Jesus, hanging on the cross, prays for the men who nailed him there. Brothers and sisters, here is my model: even when I am covered in my own mess, I still stand between other people and God. You do not have to wait until you are clean before you may intercede for someone.

The Bible is my standard — this chapter shows us the relationship between a standard and a situation. It is not that Abraham did not know lying was wrong. He assessed the situation, and then decided that this one was an exception. And what a standard means is precisely this: it does not change because of my reading of the circumstances. When you catch yourself saying, "this case is special", that is usually the exact moment the standard is being walked around.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — notice how God guides in this chapter. He did not move Abraham to repent. He moved a foreign king to dream. Brothers and sisters, this is worth being humbled by: when God stops something, he does not necessarily do it through the spiritual one in the room. Sometimes the thing that stops you is a colleague who does not believe, a remark from someone with no expertise at all, or an obstacle that appears out of nowhere.

Let Jesus be King — "because I thought, surely the fear of God is not in this place." I made God's assessment of the environment for him, and then made my own arrangements. Letting Jesus be King means I no longer let my assumptions decide whether or not to be honest. Brothers and sisters, this sentence is worth writing down: honesty is not a strategy that reads the situation. It is an identity that does not read the situation at all.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — the only one in this chapter who does nothing wrong is God. He restrains, he speaks, he protects, he heals. And of everything the human beings do, the finest single act — that prayer — was something God commanded first.

Establish God's system — God stopped Abimelech in a dream and kept the line of the promise intact. Brothers and sisters, when God protects his plan, sometimes he does not do it through us. He does it around us. That gives everyone who serves a very healthy dose of humility: this system does not hang on me. If you are tired enough today to be thinking "nothing here works without me", this chapter is the antidote written for you.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We have a very clear framework, and we have a great many testimonies and experiences. This chapter reminds us that experience is not the same thing as maturity. Abraham had been through a covenant, a change of name, circumcision, intercession, the sight of judgement — set all of that out as a list and his spiritual record is flawless. And then the first time pressure arrived he dropped straight back into the pit he had fallen into twenty-five years earlier. So please do not use a person's experiences to assess the state of his life, and do not use your own experiences as a guarantee of your tomorrow. The real test comes on the day the pressure arrives.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Old Reflex
Brothers and sisters, the same old fault, falling into four different kinds of heart, will be handled in four completely different ways.

The proud heart says, "How could Abraham possibly do that?" What this heart most wants to do when it finishes the chapter is award marks. Brothers and sisters, notice that the author of this chapter offers no verdict at all. He simply writes down what happened and lets the foreign king do the talking. And here is the thing far more worth thinking about: if even he could do this, what makes me so sure that I would not?

The fearful heart says, "So after walking with God that long you can still fall — then what hope is there for me?" To a heart like that I want to say: look at verse 7, and look at verse 17. In the very moment of his failure God still calls him a prophet, and God answers his prayer. Your office does not hang on your performance. Philippians 1:6 says that "he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ."

The ashamed heart says, "I have done the same thing again; I have no face left to pray with." Brothers and sisters, this chapter was written for you. Abraham fell into the same pit a second time, and the next assignment God handed him was — pray for somebody else. You do not have to repair yourself before you are allowed to open your mouth. And look at the first sentence of the very next chapter: "Yahweh visited Sarah as he had said, and Yahweh did to Sarah as he had spoken." The chapter after he fell is the chapter in which the promise comes true.

The wounded heart says, "And what about Sarah?" Yes. There is one person in this chapter who does not speak a single word from beginning to end, and it is the woman who was handed over as a bargaining chip. And this was the second time it had happened to her. Brothers and sisters, let me point out one thing the text does for her. In verse 16 Abimelech speaks to her — and in the whole chapter the only person who addresses Sarah directly is that foreign king. He gives her a thousand pieces of silver and tells her it is "for you a covering of the eyes to all that are with you." Even an outsider saw what her position was. God did not let the wrong done to her pass by without a sound.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, identify your own old reflex. When pressure arrives, what is the first move you most often make? Tell a lie, avoid it, lose your temper, cut off contact, work yourself into the ground, or scroll on your phone? Write it down. Recognising it is the first step in dealing with it.

Second, audit your "because I thought". This week, catch yourself in the moment you say, "I assumed that person would never …" Write down three assessments of a situation that you have already made on God's behalf, then pray over those three once, and hand the judgement back to him.

Third, be honest once without reading the situation. There will be one occasion this week where you would normally have told a half-truth — the kind where every word is accurate and the whole point is to leave the other person thinking something false. This time, say it plainly.

Fourth, serve anyway, after you have failed. If you fall this week, do not stop doing the thing you are supposed to be doing. Admit the fault, and then go back to praying for people. That is exactly how Abraham came through.

Fifth, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church this week, in three sentences. There is a great figure in the Bible who told the same lie twice, twenty-five years apart, and in between he had been through every spiritual high point you can think of. His reason was, "I assumed the people in this place had no fear of God" — and the pagan king turned out to be more upright than he was. And the part that surprised me most is that God did not replace him; God told the man he had deceived to go and ask him to pray.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that my old fault will not disappear by itself just because I have piled up experiences; I will keep watch over it.
I declare that I will no longer let my assumptions decide whether or not I am honest.
I declare that God's plan does not hang on my being perfect; he will step in and stop things, and he will even work around me.
I declare that after I have fallen I may still stand between other people and God; I will not stop interceding because I have failed.
This week I am supposed to "say one honest sentence". What if saying it really does cost me something?

Start by admitting that the cost is real. Do not wave it away with "God will make it up to you." Then do three things. First, work out whether this is something you ought to say or something you simply need not say — honesty does not mean saying everything; there are matters you have every right not to disclose. Dishonesty is saying what is false. Second, choose how you say it: a true thing can be said gently, said in the right order, and said in the right setting. Third, count the cost before you open your mouth, and be ready to carry it. And a last word about safety: if telling the truth would put you or someone else in danger — where there is violence, for instance, or an unlawful threat — seek help and protection first. That is not dishonesty. That is wisdom.
Brothers and sisters, if only one comparison from this lesson may remain, I want to leave you with two sentences.
The first is what God said in chapter 17: "Walk before me and be blameless." That word is *tamim* — whole, complete, with no piece missing.
The second is what Abimelech says in chapter 20: "I have done this in the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands." That word "integrity" is *tom* — the very same root.
God told his servant to be *tamim*; and in this chapter, the one who says of himself that he is *tom* is an outsider.
Brothers and sisters, the author set those two words down in neighbouring chapters because he means us to be embarrassed.

And the embarrassment has its uses. It stops us ever saying again, "because I am a Christian, I am the better person." People outside the church who are more honest than we are, who keep their word better than we do, who are more considerate than we are — that still happens today. When you run into it, the right response is not to explain. It is to bow your head.
But this chapter does not stop at the embarrassment. It stops at verse 17: "Abraham prayed to God. So God healed Abimelech."

God did not swap him out. God did not say, "a man like you is no longer fit to be a prophet." God had the man who had just lost every last shred of face stand up and intercede for someone else — and then answered the prayer.

Brothers and sisters, this is the hardest thing about grace to believe: it is not handed over once you have improved. It is handed to you in the very moment you have just made a mess of everything — and what it hands you is the next assignment.

And the first sentence of the next chapter is this: "Yahweh visited Sarah as he had said, and Yahweh did to Sarah as he had spoken." The chapter straight after he fell is the chapter in which the promise is fulfilled.

The focus is not on my having fallen in the same place one more time, not on how other people view my humiliation, and not on whether I am still qualified to serve. The focus is on Jesus — he is the Lord who does not replace me because I failed, and he is the High Priest who lives for ever to intercede for us. Not I, but Christ.

May God bless every one of us this week: to recognise that old reflex, and, after we have fallen, still to open our mouths and pray for other people. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at the level of mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ Twenty-five years apart, after all those experiences, the same lie came out again. What does that say about the notion that spiritual experience automatically changes a person?
2. ★★ Why is a half-truth harder to handle than an outright lie? How would you tell the two apart?
3. ★ His reason for lying was, "Because I thought, surely the fear of God is not in this place." What does that "because I thought" look like when it grows in you?
4. ★★ The first appearance of the word "prophet" in the whole Bible lands on a man who has just finished telling a lie. How does that help us hold grace and responsibility together?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I will not make the same mistake again), fearful (if I do not protect myself first I will be eaten alive), ashamed (I have fallen into the same old fault again), wounded (I have paid a price for being honest before). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Yes, I know that in the integrity of your heart you have done this, and I also withheld you from sinning against me." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ When you are backed into a corner, what is your first reaction? Run, conceal, or grit your teeth and tough it out? When did you learn that reaction?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The person I am most likely to tell half the truth to is …"
9. ★★ Which honest-but-not-rude sentence are you going to have ready this week? Say it out loud here and now, and practise it once.

Leader's reminder: question seven will touch the discouragement of falling into the same fault over and over. Do not say "you need more faith", and do not help anyone find excuses either. If someone speaks about pressure to be dishonest at work or at home, follow up with him privately after the meeting.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ Is there something at home that you have been getting past by keeping it vague? How will you say it plainly this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, in what kind of situation do you most often tell only half of it?

12. ★★★ The evidence-first practice: this week, before you put up a guard against anyone, ask one question first — "Do I have any evidence for thinking this about him?" Name someone you have written a script for recently.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him the situations in which you are most likely to be vague, and ask him to ask you about them. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there is a man in the Bible who told the same lie twice, twenty-five years apart. Second, his reason for lying was, "I assumed nobody in that place feared God" — and the pagan king turned out to be more upright than he was. Third, so what I learned is that the lies we tell to guard ourselves usually begin with an assumption that has nothing under it. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the matter you are going to say plainly this week, and the person you have written a script for. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to tear down the assumptions in our hearts that have no evidence behind them.
